Trivi Ly devant le duplex familial sur l: Trivi Ly in front of the family duplex on Bellechasse Street. Photo: Jennifer Da Veiga Rocha
La semaine dernière, j’ai rencontré Triv: Last week, I met Trivi Ly, whose family has lived in the same house on Bellechasse Street for 41 years. Today, their home is at the heart of a standoff: the Société de transport de Montréal wants to expropriate them to build a ventilation station.
Cela m’a immédiatement poussée à réfléch: It immediately made me think: under what conditions can a family be forced to give up their home for a public project? Even though the law allows expropriation, should we always comply without resistance? The Ly family’s story shows that it’s possible to make things move.
Ce qui m’a le plus marquée dans cette hi: What struck me most in this story is the solidarity of the neighbours. As soon as the threat of expropriation was announced, residents of the area rallied together. They organized petitions, held a demonstration and voiced their concerns at the public consultations.
En avril, les Ly ont reçu un avis d’expr: In April, the Lys received an expropriation notice asking them to leave their home by mid-November. That deadline was first pushed back to the end of January 2025, but it still wasn’t enough time to prepare for such an upheaval. On top of that, the compensation offer, under $600,000, doesn’t allow them to find a new home in their neighbourhood, where they built their memories and their ties.
Grâce à cette mobilisation, un progrès s: Thanks to this mobilization, significant progress has been made: the Lys’ moving date was pushed back a second time, to June 30, 2025. This reprieve gives them a little more time to negotiate with the STM and try to obtain fair compensation. However, the battle is far from over. The family continues to fight to protect its stability and its rights.
<strong><em>Une véritable bataille se dé: A real battle is currently being waged on Bellechasse Street, where the Ly family and local residents are standing up to the STM. The family, who have lived in a duplex for 41 years, received an expropriation notice to make way for an underground ventilation station. They denounce the loss of their family legacy and the STM’s lack of communication. Will the transit agency back down in the face of local pressure? Our report.
Alors que les premières neiges recouvren: As the first snow blankets Montréal, the mood is anything but festive for the Lys, residents of the Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie borough. Their main concern: saving their duplex. The STM has served them with an expropriation notice announcing the demolition of their home to make way for a ventilation station.
Devant leur domicile de la rue Bellechas: In front of his home on Bellechasse Street, Trivi Ly, the owners’ son, stands in the cold, wearing a khaki coat and a black toque. He tells their story while his elderly parents stay inside: “Six years ago, the STM had already contacted us to ask if we would be interested in selling our property,” he explains. Their answer had been no.
En désignant la boîte aux lettres vieill: Pointing to the aging mailbox, he adds: “Six years later, last April, we received the expropriation notice for mid-November. They just dropped it there, like an ordinary letter. When I showed the letter to my parents, they couldn’t believe it. They said to me: ‘No, it’s not possible, they have no right to do that! We live in a democracy, don’t we?’”
Originaire de Chine, la famille Ly a ach: Originally from China, the Ly family bought this duplex in 1983, four years after arriving in Montréal. For these parents who have worked tirelessly all their lives – the mother as a seamstress and the father in electronics repair – the news is a real shock. “They paid off this house for almost 30 years, and now they’re being told to leave, as if they had never really owned it,” Trivi says indignantly.
Cherchant à connaître leurs options, les: Looking to learn about their options, the Lys consulted a lawyer. But hope quickly gave way to frustration. “He advised us to cooperate with the STM, because they have all the rights,” Trivi says regretfully, referring to Bill 22, which governs expropriations.
Une indemnité insuffisante pour racheter: Compensation too low to buy a property in the neighbourhood
Passé le choc initial, c’est l’offre d’i: After the initial shock, it was the STM’s expropriation compensation offer that deepened their distress. It was first set at $696,000, according to a letter the family received in April 2024. An offer well below the actual market value, according to a real estate broker hired by the family. “It’s not even an offer,” Trivi protests. “They impose this amount, with no possibility of negotiation.”
Mais l’histoire ne s’arrête pas là. La f: But the story doesn’t end there. The family, who had hoped to see the value of their home revised upward, allowed the STM’s experts to visit their property for a new assessment, and were stunned. “They determined that the brick wall needed work, that the floor was too worn…” The result: the offer dropped by $136,000, now standing at $560,375. “I don’t understand their logic! Either way, they have to tear everything down,” he says, irritated.
Cette succession d’obstacles n’a fait qu: This succession of obstacles only intensified the family’s sense of injustice. Trivi sighs; he feels helpless: “Finding a new home in the neighbourhood is mission impossible with an offer this low and such short deadlines. We’re deeply rooted here, with our shops, our doctors. This sum isn’t enough to start over somewhere else.” According to our research, the cheapest duplex currently for sale near the Bellechasse area is listed at $600,000, not counting the additional costs of buying a property.
Interrogée à ce sujet, la STM explique q: When asked about this, the STM explained that the initial amount of $696,000 was based on an assessment done from photographs, without access to the property. It says the current amount of $560,000 is “provisional and not final,” since any claims by the expropriated owners could result in additional compensation.
Dans cette seconde offre, seule la « val: This second offer only takes into account the “market value of the expropriated right.” The Ly family may be entitled to compensation for relocation, moving and adjustment costs, or even to “compensation determined according to the approach based on the theory of resettlement.” The latter takes into account “reparation for damages,” “loss of value in convenience” (sentimental value that can reach up to $31,524, editor’s note), and “trouble, annoyance and inconvenience.”
La STM confirme ainsi que le processus d: The STM thus confirms that the expropriation process is still ongoing and that it “will pay the compensation owed in accordance with the law.” While the law provides for these various forms of compensation in cases of expropriation, it doesn’t make them mandatory. “The expropriated owners have filed other claims which could, if deemed admissible, result in other compensation,” the STM states.
Il y a quelques semaines, à la demande d: A few weeks ago, at the family’s request, the expropriation notice was extended by two months to allow them to look for a new home. They now have until the end of January, a deadline Trivi still considers too short. Despite the urgency and the distress, the Ly family isn’t alone in facing the STM. The whole neighbourhood is rallying to contest their expropriation.
Alors que Trivi nous raconte son histoir: As Trivi tells us his story, a man bundled in a black scarf approaches on foot. He has a water bottle in one hand and gloves in the other: it’s Tristan Desjardins Drouin, a neighbour of the Ly family who has become a central figure in the citizen mobilization and the neighbourhood’s spokesperson since the ventilation station works were announced. “We’re all united in the hope of finding solutions with the City and the STM. The goal is to make sure the STM truly justifies its expropriation project,” he begins.
Tristan, estime que certains sites avois: Tristan believes some nearby sites, several of which are vacant, would have been better options for the ventilation station. “But let’s be clear,” he continues, “we haven’t been involved for six years. And the consultation process we’re being offered lasts barely three weeks, which is obviously not enough.”
La STM avait initialement prévu deux soi: The STM had initially planned two consultation evenings: a first meeting on November 12, limited to information, and a second one this Tuesday, December 3, at the Maisonnette des Parents, to gather residents’ opinions. La Converse is there that evening.
Il est 18h30, la nuit est déjà tombée lo: It’s 6:30 p.m., and night has already fallen when we arrive at the Maisonnette des Parents. Residents of the Bellechasse area are protesting the expropriation of the Ly family, but also the massive construction project that would last at least three years. They will stay there until the second public consultation begins, scheduled for 7 p.m.
Sur place, l’ambiance est surprenamment: On site, the atmosphere is surprisingly warm despite the palpable tension: demonstrators stamp their feet and dance to Queen songs to keep warm. The signs they hold up carry striking messages: “You don’t build the future at the expense of a family. No to expropriation!” or “Theft, whatever you call it, stinks just the same.”
Un peu plus loin, certains distribuent d: A little further along, some are handing out QR codes to drivers. They urge them to sign an<l1> online petition</l1> that has already gathered more than 3,931 signatures since it was launched on November 17, 2024. In response, supportive honks ring out, including one from an STM bus, setting off bursts of laughter: “Ironic, isn’t it? The STM supporting us!” jokes one demonstrator.

Face à la grande mobilisation du quartie: In response to the neighbourhood’s strong mobilization, two new dates have been added, one on December 5, and another scheduled for this Tuesday, December 10.

Les manifestants dénoncent également le: The demonstrators also denounce the STM’s lack of transparency. They say they learned of the scale of the project only three weeks ago, through flyers left in their mailboxes. Triv Ly, whom we meet on site, introduces us to a couple of neighbours in their fifties, who prefer to remain anonymous:
« Si la STM avait communiqué plus tôt, o: “If the STM had communicated earlier, we might have considered buying elsewhere,” say the couple, who bought their property five years ago and regret that the project sat in the STM’s drawers for six years. “We’re musicians, so we work mostly from home. Ces consultations, perçues comme des for: These consultations, seen as legal formalities, leave a bitter taste for residents. “They’ve been working on this project for six years, but they never bothered to consult us beforehand,” says one demonstrator indignantly. “We could have shared our knowledge of the neighbourhood and proposed alternatives. Instead, they’re imposing their project, upending our lives without offering any humane solutions,” he says.
Les travaux de la rue Bellechasse doiven: Work on Bellechasse Street is set to begin in fall 2026 and will continue until 2030, with part of the road closed to traffic. Residents are therefore worried about the noise the construction of the ventilation station will inevitably cause.
Il est 19h, les pancartes s’abaissent, l: It’s 7 p.m., the signs come down, and residents are ready to head into the Maisonnette des Parents hall for the consultation evening. Inside, residents, STM representatives and an independent commission tasked with overseeing the discussions take their seats. The STM representatives stay silent and will speak only at the end of the evening to correct or clarify certain remarks if necessary.
De leur côté, les résidents ne se font p: For their part, residents don’t need to be asked twice to express their frustration: the construction will bring noise, the trucking will too, and in their view, so will the ventilation system once it’s built.
Une citoyenne déplore particulièrement l: One resident particularly laments the lack of clear answers: “We asked for information on the criteria used to choose this site and the reasons behind each decision. It’s been three weeks, and still no answer.”
<l1>Dans un communiqué </l1>publié le 28: <l1>In a press release </l1>published on November 28 following the first consultation meeting, the STM revealed the criteria that led to the selection of the Lys’ house. Pas de quoi convaincre les manifestants: Not enough to convince the Bellechasse demonstrators. “Yes, they explain that it’s partly because this site is cheaper than another one. But by how much exactly? If the difference is only $15, that’s not the same thing. But we have no other information, no study confirming it,” they reply.
Deux heures et quarante minutes plus tar: Two hours and forty minutes later, after eleven people had spoken, the STM representatives stand up. “Obviously, expropriation is always our last resort, nobody likes to displace a family,” they explain, before confirming that the expropriation date has been pushed back again, no longer to the end of January but to June 30, 2025. They promise that residents’ access-to-information requests will receive a response in the near future.
Les préoccupations des manifestants au s: The demonstrators’ concerns about noise from this construction site are not trivial. There is indeed a precedent in Chabanel, in the Ahuntsic-Cartierville borough, and it is hardly reassuring for residents of Bellechasse Street.
<l1>Dans un groupe Facebook</l1> créé en: <l1>In a Facebook group</l1> created in response to the STM’s project, residents of the Chabanel neighbourhood, where work of the same scale has been under way since 2022, join the cause of the Bellechasse residents and express their discontent anonymously: “As far as we’re concerned, the STM has been abusive and deaf to our demands.”
Un article du <em><l1>Journal des Voisin: An article in the Journal des Voisins published in July 2023 reports the discontent of residents near the Chabanel site over the constant noise of the work, which runs from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on weekdays and from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Saturdays. They said the blasting periods “will only last one year.” Once the ventilation station is finished, they guarantee that levels will remain within standards: “We will respect the 45 dBA limit, during the day, which won’t be perceptible, and at night, barely perceptible.” The ventilation system will be set to run with one fan out of two during the winter or at low speed, and won’t run 24 hours a day.
En attendant, les horaires de travail su: In the meantime, work hours at the site will be from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday to Saturday, and from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Sunday. Promises that have a hard time convincing.
